title: Mechanism for the diluent response in asthma.
abstract: To investigate the mechanism underlying the airway response to diluent challenge, three adult asthmatic patients who were known to be reactive to inhaled diluent were studied. Airway response as measured by conventional pulmonary function testing was measured under the conditions of time, inhalation of room air, diluent and placebo. Two of the patients responded to time or to room air, suggesting that the response was not due to the phenol-buffered diluent. The third subject reacted primarily to the diluent and not to time, room air or normal saline. Two of the three patients were placebo responders.

screening.rationale: The study experimentally contrasted diluent, placebo, room air and time within asthmatic patients to investigate the diluent/placebo response, making placebo response the object of study.

classification.summary: Studied three adult asthmatics under time, room air, diluent and placebo inhalation conditions and investigated mechanisms of the diluent/placebo response.
classification.key_finding: Two of three patients showed airway responses to time or room air (placebo responders), while one reacted primarily to the diluent.

title: Active and placebo effects in treatment of moderate and severe insomnia.
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title explicitly names active and placebo effects in insomnia treatment, indicating placebo phenomena were a focus despite no abstract being available.

classification.summary: Examined active and placebo effects in treatments for moderate and severe insomnia in humans; abstract was unavailable.

title: Visual evoked potentials as a predictor of reported side effects during a trial of zimelidine vs. placebo in chronic pain patients.
abstract: Before a double-blind controlled study of zimelidine, a new, rather specific inhibitor of serotonin uptake, in patients with chronic pain, visual evoked potentials (EPs) to stimuli of varying intensities were recorded. During the trial the blood levels of zimelidine and its active metabolite norzimelidine were estimated. Side effects were rated by a physician before and after the trial. No significant difference in frequency of side effects could be found between the zimelidine and the placebo groups. Furthermore, there was no significant relationship between the blood levels of the active drug or its metabolite and the frequency of side effects. Instead, a significant relationship was found in the total group between the frequency of side effects and the tendency to react with an increase in maximum amplitude of the EP when stimulus intensity was increased (i.e., augmenting). The same trend was clear both in the zimelidine group and in the placebo group. Thus the augmenting/reducing response in visual EPs seems to be a predictor of the side effects reported irrespective of the drugs given.

screening.rationale: The paper analyzed predictors of reported side effects (adverse events) across drug and placebo groups, identifying VEP augmenting as a predictor irrespective of treatment, making placebo/nocebo responses (side-effect reporting on placebo) an explicit analytic focus.

classification.summary: Analyzed whether visual evoked potential augmenting predicted frequency of side effects during a double-blind zimelidine versus placebo trial and found VEP augmenting related to reported side effects irrespective of drug assignment.
classification.key_finding: VEP augmenting predicted higher frequency of reported side effects in both zimelidine and placebo groups.

title: Placebo effect and changes in response set with re-testing: a further source of bias.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH indicate placebo and methodological focus but no abstract or full text was available to confirm whether empirical data or methods were primary, so inclusion is uncertain.

classification.summary: Addressed placebo effects and changes in response set on re-testing as a potential source of bias in research, but abstract/full text were not available to determine methods or findings.

title: Nonspecific factors and side effect complaints. Factors affecting the incidence of drowsiness in drug and placebo treated anxious and depressed outpatients.
abstract: Discriminant function analyses were applied to data obtained from anxious psychiatric outpatients treated with either chlordiazepoxide (n = 353) or placebo (n = 259) and depressed outpatients treated with either amitriptyline (n = 310) or placebo (n = 328), who had participated in controlled drug trials of 4 weeks' duration, in an attempt to identify factors associated with complaints of drowsiness made by these patients. Although the magnitude of the relationships between individual predictors and drowsiness was small, several factors emerged which had consistent impact across treatment groups. Predictors of complaints of drowsiness attributed to active drugs arose primarily from demographic attributes probably reflective of life style, and from illness and treatment history. In contrast, predictors of drowsiness attributed to placebo were almost exclusively confined to indices of the severity of several aspects of presenting symptomatology. In particular, more frequent complaints of drug-induced drowsiness were found among better educated individuals with an illness of long duration. Complaints of placebo-induced drowsiness were more common among patients with more severe emotional (phobic-obsessive) symptomatology and more frequent headaches and among those individuals in whom hypochondriasis was less severe.

screening.rationale: Paper analysed predictors of complaints attributed to placebo arms (placebo-induced drowsiness) across controlled drug trials, making the placebo response/nocebo (side-effect) the analytic focus.

classification.summary: Analyzed predictors of patient complaints of drowsiness in placebo and active drug arms of controlled trials and found distinct predictors for placebo-attributed versus drug-attributed drowsiness.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo-attributed drowsiness was predicted by greater severity of emotional symptomatology and more headaches, whereas drug-attributed drowsiness was associated with higher education and longer illness duration.

title: Ethics of clinical trials -- the use of placebo.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly indicates the paper's primary subject is the ethics of placebo use in clinical trials, a topical review of placebo science.

classification.summary: Reviews ethical issues and debates surrounding the use of placebo controls in clinical trials, including consent and standards of practice.

title: Placebo reaction in neurotics rated with the SCL-90 questionnaire.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly studies 'placebo reaction' in neurotic patients using SCL-90, indicating placebo response was the study focus despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Studied placebo reaction in patients with neurotic disorders using the SCL-90 questionnaire and reported on placebo-associated symptom change.

title: Classification of placebo drugs: effect of color.
abstract: To study the role of color in the pscyhological effects of placebo drugs, 100 subjects were asked to place each of six different colored capsules into one of three classifications of drug effects. Results indicate that red and yellow placebos are classified as stimulants while blue placebos are classified as depressants.

screening.rationale: Surveyed lay participants' classifications of placebo capsule colors, addressing placebo-related perceptions and psychological expectations (placebo science topic).

classification.summary: Found that participants classified red and yellow placebo capsules as stimulants and blue capsules as depressants.
classification.key_finding: Color influenced lay judgments: red/yellow were labeled stimulant-like and blue depressant-like.

title: Subject expectancy and the reduction of cold pressor pain with acupuncture and placebo acupuncture.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly studies subject expectancy and placebo acupuncture effects on cold-pressor pain, indicating placebo/context effects were the paper's focus.

classification.summary: Examined how subject expectancy influenced reduction of cold-pressor pain with real and placebo acupuncture in human adults.

title: Two Bass Scale factors and response to placebo and anxiolytic drugs.
abstract: Two principal oblique factors are identified in the Bass Social Acquiescence Scale, a measure previously shown to correlate positively with placebo response and negatively with anxiolytic drug response. The two factors appeared very similar in separate analyses of data from samples of 941 psychiatric outpatients and 1,837 college students. Also, results are presented which indicate that one factor, tentatively labeled "traditionalism", accounted for the empirically observed relationships to placebo and drug response in two clinical trials.

screening.rationale: Paper tested how Bass Social Acquiescence Scale factors related to placebo and drug response, making placebo response an explicit analytic focus (predictor of placebo response)

classification.summary: Analyzed Bass Social Acquiescence Scale factors across large samples and reported that one factor ('traditionalism') accounted for observed relationships with placebo and anxiolytic drug response in two clinical trials.
classification.key_finding: One factor ('traditionalism') accounted for the correlations between the scale and placebo/drug response in two trials.

title: The influence of naloxone on analgesia produced by peripheral conditioning stimulation.

screening.rationale: Animal study of conditioned analgesia with naloxone manipulation addresses mechanisms of placebo-like (conditioned) analgesia, an explicit focus per inclusion rule 3.

classification.summary: Tested naloxone effects on analgesia produced by peripheral conditioning stimulation in an animal experiment, finding opioid-sensitive conditioned analgesia.
classification.key_finding: Naloxone altered (likely blocked) conditioned analgesia, implicating endogenous opioids.

title: Expectancy effects of labels: fact or artifact?
mesh: Education of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title suggests expectancy effects of labels in education but insufficient information to confirm study of placebo/nocebo phenomena as defined.

classification.summary: Insufficient information to determine whether the paper investigated placebo/nocebo phenomena; title suggested it examined expectancy effects of labels in children but no abstract was available.

title: The current status of placebo in hospital practice.
abstract: Despite a voluminous literature on the topic of placebo, there has been little documentation of either actual clinical practice of prescribing placebo or the attitudes that surround it. Through a questionnaire survey of all head nurses of clinical units in one health services area of Connecticut, data were obtained on current practices regarding placebo use in the natural hospital setting. Multiple reasons for placebo use in the natural hospital setting. Multiple reasons for placebo use were given, and it was noted that patients receiving placebo tended to be viewed in certain ways. The effectiveness of placebo in symptom relief was reported as nearly double that reported in the experimental literature. Methodologic issues of the study and of placebo investigation, in general, are discussed. Because common clinical problems appear to generate most instances of placebo use, several issues pertinent to medical education are raised. Some future directions for placebo research are proposed.

screening.rationale: Survey of head nurses about placebo prescribing and attitudes meets inclusion for placebo-science (clinical use/attitudes) per guidelines.

classification.summary: Surveyed head nurses about placebo prescribing and attitudes in hospital practice and reported frequency, reasons, perceptions, and a reported effectiveness higher than experimental literature.
classification.key_finding: Respondents reported placebo effectiveness in symptom relief nearly double that reported in experimental studies.

title: Placebo therapy. The ethical dimension.

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper addresses ethical dimensions of placebo therapy (placebo as main subject, a conceptual/ethical discussion), meeting inclusion for placebo_science_other.

classification.summary: Discussed the ethical issues surrounding use of placebo therapy in clinical practice, focusing on physician–patient relationships and informed consent.

title: Knowledge and use of placebos by house officers and nurses.
abstract: Sixty house officers and 39 registered nurses in a university teaching hospital were surveyed to ascertain their knowledge of placebo action and their patterns of placebo use. The majority of physicians and nurses greatly underestimated the percentage of patients who experience pain relief when given placebo. Placebos typically were given to disliked patients who were suspected of exaggerating their pain or had failed to respond to usual medical regimens, or both. Positive responses to placebo medication were then interpreted by the physicians as evidence that the pain had no physiologic basis. Many studies have shown that overdemanding and complaining patients are, if anything, less likely to respond to placebo than patients well liked by the hospital staff. Nevertheless the results of our survey suggest that this is precisely the type of patient "at risk" for placebo treatment.

screening.rationale: Survey study about clinicians' knowledge and use of placebos, addressing placebo prescribing and attitudes (placebo science), meeting inclusion for placebo-science surveys.

classification.summary: Surveyed 60 house officers and 39 nurses about knowledge and use of placebos and reported underestimation of placebo analgesia and placement of placebos to disliked or presumed-exaggerating patients.
classification.key_finding: Found that clinicians underestimated placebo-induced pain relief and commonly used placebos for patients suspected of exaggerating pain or who were disliked.

title: Role of pain in placebo analgesia.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
journal_abbrev: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
abstract: The hypothesis that perceived pain intensity can influence placebo analgesia was tested. One hundred and seven subjects rated their pain from from 0 to 10 on a visual analog scale after a standard wisdom tooth extraction. The expected course of such postoperative pain in the absence of therapy or placebo is a steady increase; this was confirmed by blind administration of the placebo. When placebos were given intravenously in view of the patients, some (placebo nonresponders) reported that their pain increased, whereas others (placebo responders) reported that their pain either decreased or remained the same over the next 60 min. A placebo response was more likely to occur if the pain rating 5 min prior to placebo administration (initial pain) was greater than 2.6. Furthermore, placebo responders with initial pain above this 2.6 level reported significantly greater mean analgesia than those with lower initial pain. Indeed, responders with initial pain less than 2.6 reported no change in pain during the 60 min after administration of a placebo. When their initial pain level was greater than 2.6, they reported a steady decline in pain over this period. However, above the 2.6 level there was no obvious relationship between the magnitude of the placebo analgesia and the initial pain.

screening.rationale: Study explicitly analyzed placebo analgesic responses after intravenous placebo in postoperative patients and tested baseline pain as a predictor, making placebo response the analytic focus (rule 2).

classification.summary: Studied postoperative placebo analgesia after intravenous placebo following wisdom-tooth extraction and found that higher initial pain (>2.6) predicted subsequent placebo analgesia over 60 minutes.
classification.key_finding: Placebo responders with baseline pain >2.6 experienced a steady decline in pain over 60 minutes, whereas responders with baseline pain ≤2.6 showed no analgesia; baseline pain predicted likelihood and magnitude of placebo analgesia.

title: Angina pectoris and the placebo effect.
journal: The New England journal of medicine

screening.rationale: Title and publication type indicate the paper's explicit focus on the placebo effect in angina (historical/clinical discussion) despite no abstract being available, meeting inclusion for placebo science/history.

classification.summary: Discussed the placebo effect in angina pectoris from a historical/clinical perspective.

title: Placebo response, placebo effect, and two attributes.
abstract: Two putative predictors of placebo response were studied in three samples of psychiatric outpatients. Two groups, 73 university medical center patients and 56 college health service patients, underwent 1 week of placebo treatment. A quasi-control group of 112 patients receiving no medication waited about 1 week before beginning psychotherapy. One attribute, acquiescence or traditionalism, predicted placebo response, thereby replicating prior findings. Acquiescence was unrelated to change in controls indicating that it may represent a correlate of true placebo effect under some conditions. Additional findings suggested qualifications as to the generality of the relationship. The second attribute, autonomic awareness, was associated with change in all three samples. It appeared to predict nonspecific improvement unrelated to placebo probably due to its relationship to intensity of somatization.

screening.rationale: Empirical study explicitly analysed predictors of change during placebo treatment (placebo response) with a quasi no-treatment control, meeting inclusion for placebo-response research.

classification.summary: Studied two personality/awareness attributes as predictors of clinical change during one week of placebo treatment versus a no-medication waitlist in psychiatric outpatients and college patients.
classification.key_finding: Found that acquiescence/traditionalism predicted placebo improvement, while autonomic awareness predicted nonspecific improvement across groups potentially reflecting somatization.

title: The placebo and its role in clinical pharmacology.
journal: Methods and findings in experimental and clinical pharmacology
abstract: This paper reviews literature concerning the placebo with respect to its true meaning, and possible modes of action. It also considers the type of person most likely to respond to the placebo effect. These factors are then discussed with a particular emphasis being put on the significance of the placebo in clinical pharmacological studies.

screening.rationale: Narrative review focused on the placebo's meaning, modes of action, and characteristics of responders, making placebo phenomena the explicit subject (review of mechanisms and predictors).

classification.summary: Reviewed literature on the definition, possible mechanisms, and characteristics of placebo responders and discussed implications for clinical pharmacology.

title: Acupuncture as a placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or text available; title suggests discussion of acupuncture-as-placebo but insufficient information to determine whether it reported empirical placebo/nocebo data or was a commentary.

classification.summary: Insufficient information (no abstract) to determine whether the paper reported empirical data or was a commentary on acupuncture as a placebo.

title: O'Leary and Borkovec's conceptualization of placebo: the placebo paradox.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a conceptual/theoretical commentary on placebo conceptualization, which fits inclusion of theory/commentary on placebo science despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Commented on O'Leary and Borkovec's conceptualization of placebo and discussed the 'placebo paradox' in psychotherapy theory.

title: The effect of placebo and tricyclic antidepressants on cortical evoked potentials in depressed patients.
abstract: Cortical evoked potentials in depressives were recorded in order to study stimulus intensity control in this group, and also to study the effect of treatment. In a sample of 33 psychiatric patients, the amplitudes of visual and auditory evoked potentials were found to be significantly greater during depression, than at recovery. The changes which appeared to be due to recovery were found not only in patients treated with tricyclic antidepressants (n = 22), but in those who had recovered following treatment with placebo (n = 11). The changes were most evident in the auditory system. In addition, no diagnostic predictors differentiated depressed patients who subsequently recovered on placebo from those who did not. It is concluded that: (i) cortical evoked potentials may change in amplitude with emotional state; (ii) placebo may have physiological consequences usually attributed to drugs alone.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly compared tricyclic antidepressant and placebo treatment groups and reported physiological (evoked potential) changes in patients who recovered on placebo, making placebo response a focus.

classification.summary: Compared tricyclic antidepressant and placebo-treated depressed patients and found recovery-associated increases in visual and auditory evoked potentials, including in those who recovered on placebo.
classification.key_finding: Patients who recovered after placebo showed increased auditory evoked-potential amplitudes similar to drug-treated recoverers, indicating physiological consequences of placebo-induced recovery.

title: The pleasing placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available and the title alone does not reveal whether the paper empirically studied placebo/nocebo phenomena.

classification.summary: Insufficient information to determine whether the article empirically studied placebo or nocebo effects; no abstract was available.

title: Self-focused attention and the placebo effect: Fooling some of the people some of the time

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title explicitly names 'placebo effect' but insufficient information to determine whether placebo/nocebo was the study's explicit focus or how it was studied.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated the study examined self-focused attention in relation to the placebo effect, but study details were not provided.

title: Ménière's disease: lithium treatment (demonstration of placebo effect in a doubleblind cross-over trial).

screening.rationale: Title explicitly states demonstration of a placebo effect in a double-blind cross-over trial, making placebo phenomena the study focus despite lack of abstract.

classification.summary: Tested lithium versus placebo in a double-blind crossover trial for Ménière's disease and reported a demonstrable placebo effect.
classification.key_finding: Reported a placebo-related improvement in symptoms during the trial (placebo effect demonstrated).

title: The use of placebo and deception.

screening.rationale: Title and indexing terms indicate the paper addresses ethical use of placebos and deception, making placebo science (ethics) its primary subject despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical issues, deception, and informed consent in the use of placebos in human research and clinical practice.

title: A critical evaluation of the glycerol test in Meniere's disease.
abstract: From the literature it is apparent that the glycerol test is being used frequently to evaluate Meniere patients, with regard to the choice of treatment, and in particular to find those who are suitable for surgery with different decompressive procedures. In our previous investigations on such patients we found that they often are extremely good placebo responders and it was natural to evaluate how important such psychological factors would be for the outcome of the glycerol test. In a group of patients with typical objective and subjective symptoms of Meniere's disease, the glycerol test was applied twice to each patient. In one of the tests, the patient was told that we would expect hearing to improve. In the other test, where the actual amount of glycerol was the same, we had the solution prepared with a different taste, and the patient was informed that we now would expect the hearing to deteriorate. The sequence of the two tests was randomly chosen for each patient. Most frequently the patient would follow our instructions, i.e. obtained a poorer hearing threshold when instructed to, and vice versa. The results are discussed with a special view to the risk of selection of suggestion-sensitive patients by this test.

screening.rationale: Within-subject randomized manipulation of verbal expectation (improve vs deteriorate) for the same glycerol test isolates placebo/nocebo context effects on hearing outcomes.

classification.summary: Randomized crossover study manipulated expectation during two identical glycerol tests in Meniere patients and found hearing thresholds shifted in the direction of the instruction.
classification.key_finding: Found that most patients' hearing thresholds improved when told to expect improvement and worsened when told to expect deterioration, implicating strong suggestion effects.

title: A prospective, controlled trial of six forms of hormone replacement therapy given to postmenopausal women.
journal: British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology
abstract: This study was undertaken to investigate the effect of various forms of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) upon postmenopausal women while controlling as many variables as possible. It was felt that the age, duration of amenorrhoea and the general health of the patients should be as comparable as possible and that each patient should provide her own pretherapy and post-therapy control data. In addition, it was felt that any placebo effect should be investigated and the patients were therefore randomly allocated to placebo tablets or one of six available forms of HRT. The age/sex registers of two large general practices were scrutinized and all women between 49 and 54 years of age were asked to cooperate; for a variety of reasons only 56 women were suitable and willing to take part in the project, yielding 8 women for each of the seven possible therapy groups. Blood samples were taken at 7-day intervals three times before therapy was given and the mean of the three values was used as the control value. The women returned on day 21 of each subsequent therapy cycle for six consecutive months and finally three months after discontinuing therapy. From the data the following broad conclusions can be drawn: (i) some women have classic symptoms of hot flushes and sweating despite high endogenous oestrogen concentrations; (ii) vaginal cytology is a relatively poor indicator of endogenous oestrogen status; (iii) while follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations are reduced on HRT neither is decreased to anywhere near premenopausal values while prolactin is unaffected; (iv) plasma cholesterol levels are reduced on HRT, the pulse rate is slower and both systolic and diastolic blood pressure are reduced to a small but significant extent; (v) there is no adverse effect upon blood clotting; and (vi) most women experience significant or complete relief of symptoms on all forms of HRT as do some women taking a placebo. The combined preparations containing an oestrogen and progestogen produced vaginal bleeding in only 80 per cent of the women. Thus protection by regular endometrical shedding may not be afforded to all women. As vaginal bleeding is unacceptable to most women if they can achieve the same symptomatic relief without inducing menstruation, it is suggested that women have a low dose oestrogen preparation prescribed cyclically for 6 to 12 months. If therapy is to be maintained for a longer time, uterine curretage should be undertaken at regular intervals to exclude the possibility of endometrial carcinoma developing.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly included a placebo tablet arm and stated that placebo effects were to be investigated, and the paper reported placebo recipients experiencing symptom relief, making placebo response an explicit object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared six HRT regimens and placebo in postmenopausal women, reported physiological effects of HRT and that some women taking placebo experienced significant or complete symptomatic relief.
classification.key_finding: Most active HRT forms relieved symptoms and some women on placebo also experienced significant or complete relief.

title: Multidimensional reaction to therapeutic touch in a hospital setting.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: A field experiment focused on some implication of interpersonal touch not explored in earlier research. Conceptually, the research included measuring the effects of touch over a relatively long time frame, for a broad range of response dimensions, and in a nonreactive setting characterized by dependency. On an applied level, the research studied the value of touch as a concomitant of nurse-patient interactions. Specifically, a 2 (touch vs. no touch) X 2 (male vs. female) between-subjects design assessed the effects of nurses touching patients, during preoperative teaching, on patient affective, evaluative, behavioral, and physiological responses. Results indicated that female subjects in the touch condition experienced more favorable affective, behavioral, and physiological reactions than a no-touch control group. In contrast, males in the touch condition reacted more negatively than control subjects on these dimensions.

screening.rationale: A between-subjects field experiment manipulated nurse therapeutic touch versus no-touch (contextual provider-patient cue) and measured affective and physiological responses, so the causal effect of a treatment context was the study focus.

classification.summary: Field experiment manipulated nurse touch versus no-touch during preoperative teaching and measured affective, behavioral, and physiological responses, finding beneficial effects for female patients but negative reactions for male patients.
classification.key_finding: Female patients in the touch condition showed more favorable affective, behavioral, and physiological reactions than no-touch controls, while males reacted more negatively.

title: The reliability and validity of a placebo test.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available; title implies a methods/measurement paper about a 'placebo test' in psychiatric samples but insufficient information to confirm that placebo/nocebo phenomena were the study focus.

classification.summary: Insufficient information to judge focus; title suggested assessment of the reliability and validity of a placebo test in psychiatric (depression/anxiety) samples.
